claim: Duration as % price change per 1-point yield move; "also equals" weighted average time; coupon/maturity effects; zero-coupon.

edits.old: Duration is the measure that turns this idea into a number. In plain words, duration is the approximate percentage change in a bond's price for a one-percentage-point change in its yield. A bond with a duration of 2 moves roughly 2 percent for each point; a bond with a duration of 15 moves roughly 15 percent. Duration is measured in years because it also equals the weighted average time until the bond's cash comes back. Longer maturity and lower coupon both push duration up, because more of the value sits in the distant future. A zero-coupon bond, which pays nothing until maturity, has a duration equal to its full maturity.
edits.new: Duration is the measure that turns this idea into a number. In plain words, duration is the approximate percentage change in a bond's price for a one-percentage-point change in its yield. A bond with a duration of 2 moves roughly 2 percent for each point; a bond with a duration of 15 moves roughly 15 percent. Duration is quoted in years because it is closely tied to the weighted average time until the bond's cash comes back. Longer maturity and lower coupon both push duration up, because more of the value sits in the distant future. A zero-coupon bond, which pays nothing until maturity, has a duration equal to its full maturity.

note: The price-sensitivity measure (modified duration) equals the weighted average time (Macaulay duration) divided by (1 + yield per period), so it does not exactly equal it. Reworded to "closely tied". Other statements correct.

claim: FRBSF 2018: every recession in ~60 years preceded by negative spread, one false positive; Cleveland: last eight recessions, "several inversions" not followed.

edits.old: The historical record is what makes the topic famous. In a 2018 Economic Letter, economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco documented that every U.S. recession in the preceding sixty years had been preceded by a negative term spread, and that a negative spread was followed by a recession in all but one case. The Cleveland Fed's yield-curve page likewise records that inversions preceded each of the last eight recessions, while also listing several inversions that were not followed by one, including the long inversion that ran from late 2022 into 2024. The pattern is real, and so are the exceptions.
edits.new: The historical record is what makes the topic famous. In a 2018 Economic Letter, economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco documented that every U.S. recession in the preceding sixty years had been preceded by a negative term spread, and that a negative spread was followed by a recession in all but one case. The Cleveland Fed's yield-curve page likewise records that inversions preceded each of the last eight recessions, while also listing three notable false signals, including the long inversion that ran from late 2022 through late 2024. The pattern is real, and so are the exceptions.

note: FRBSF (Jan 1955-Feb 2018) supports the first sentence. Cleveland lists three false positives: late-1966 inversion, a very flat curve (not an inversion) in late 1998, and late 2022 through late 2024. "Several inversions" and "into 2024" were inaccurate.

edits.old: The record above is a description of the past, not a forecast. Inversions have come before recessions with gaps ranging from a few months to about two years, some inversions were not followed by any recession, and the economy has changed in ways that could weaken or strengthen the link. claim: 5% nominal minus 3% inflation ≈ 2% real; negative real yield when inflation exceeds nominal.

edits.old: The yield printed on a bond is a nominal yield: the percentage of money you receive, counted in dollars. It says nothing about what those dollars buy. If a bond yields 5 percent while prices in the shops rise 3 percent, the lender's purchasing power grows by only about 2 percent. That leftover is the real yield. As a rule of thumb, real yield is roughly the nominal yield minus the inflation rate. When inflation runs above the nominal yield, the real yield is negative, and the lender ends up able to buy less than before even though the account balance grew.
edits.new: The yield printed on a bond is a nominal yield: the percentage of money you receive, counted in dollars. It says nothing about what those dollars buy. If a bond yields 5 percent while prices in stores rise 3 percent, the lender's purchasing power grows by only about 2 percent. That leftover is the real yield. As a rule of thumb, real yield is roughly the nominal yield minus the inflation rate. When inflation runs above the nominal yield, the real yield is negative, and the lender ends up able to buy less than before even though the account balance grew.

note: Arithmetic correct. "Prices in the shops" is British usage; changed to US "in stores".

claim: Short rates track short end; mortgages track long yields; Fed calls chain transmission "usually with a lag of months or longer".

edits.old: The policy rate matters to households because other rates are priced off the curve. Savings accounts, money market funds and short certificates of deposit tend to track the short end, so their rates move soon after the FOMC acts. A 30-year fixed mortgage is priced closer to long Treasury yields, which is why mortgage rates can move before a policy meeting, on expectations, and sometimes barely react to the meeting itself. The Federal Reserve describes this chain as the transmission of monetary policy: a change at the short end works its way through financial conditions to spending, hiring and prices, usually with a lag of months or longer.
edits.new: The policy rate matters to households because other rates are priced off the curve. Savings accounts, money market funds and short certificates of deposit tend to track the short end, so their rates move soon after the FOMC acts. A 30-year fixed mortgage is priced closer to long Treasury yields, which is why mortgage rates can move before a policy meeting, on expectations, and sometimes barely react to the meeting itself. The Federal Reserve describes this chain as the transmission of monetary policy: a change at the short end works its way through financial conditions to spending, hiring and prices, and those effects build over time.

note: Fed page uses "transmission of monetary policy" and says effects arrive "over time" but states no lag length; the sentence attributed a months-long lag to the Fed. Reworded to match the cited page.
